message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
Here is what I recall, section by section. Wording is paraphrased unless quoted, and the quotes may not be exact. The full text is still earlier in our conversation, so this tests my attention to it more than my memory in the human sense.

**Title and introduction**
- Titled "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It covers how to work with the team's material and with colleagues.
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight.
- Part of that weight comes from the evidence, and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Colleagues who have worked in an area for years have usually tested their conclusions in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence "is itself evidence," since it reflects checks they have already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common:
  - overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected;
  - understating is "more insidious," because a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little and undermine work done well.
- **Example:** a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports that its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2. Take in what was said before you answer**
- Before responding, make sure you have taken the material in, and show it: restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This is "not politeness"; it keeps a conversation moving rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find the part that's right, say so, and extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement make people defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement "is the ground, not the contribution." The useful reply is the next step the shared understanding makes available.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Your reply confirms the direction, picks up what you can act on now, and says the budget will follow "in due course."

**§3. Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- The value of a shared record is that the team builds on it together.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into "private versions of the truth" and stops being able to act.
- **Example:** before citing a report summarised as "costs fell 12%" in a budget meeting, make sure you are quoting the summary accurately.

**§4. Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions are settled and some less certain. Mark which is which, then keep the work moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block dependent decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on. It can be revisited if something new comes up, whereas a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping a question open because one more check feels safer, is "the more common one in careful people." It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed and save your energy for live questions.
- **Example:** a trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

**§5. Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues, and those from other parts of the organisation, often see the material differently. That is valuable only if their time goes where it is useful.
- A reviewer who starts from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.
- So when you ask someone to check your work, give them context: what you've concluded, where you see the risks, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds the issues faster.
- In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

**§6. Make your moves where they will land well**
- Before taking a step you can see is good, check that it fits what the people who own the area have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating them, make the call once the direction is confirmed, and release the result when it's ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone, which costs more than a short conversation beforehand.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position; the owner can see considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely: small, routine steps don't need sign-off. But the default for steps that matter is to check first, then act together.
- **Example:** rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

**§7. Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push you toward the other.
- The pairs:
  - **Overclaiming / second-guessing:** overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
  - **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one:** finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous; missing one that is.
  - **Closing too early / keeping open too long:** declaring a question answered prematurely; refusing to accept the answer the team has reached.
  - **Abandoning a line / relitigating one:** dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening one already decided.
  - **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively:** accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
  - **Acting alone / waiting too long:** making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps already agreed.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, "the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

**A last word**
- This isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work going well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team itself: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and an agreed direction.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."
